display_title: Scottish Islanders Face Record Fuel Costs
display_title_he: תושבי האיים בסקוטלנד מתמודדים עם מחירי דלק שיא
short_summary: Inhabitants of remote Scottish islands are grappling with the highest diesel prices in the UK, putting a heavy financial squeeze on commuting, public services, and daily life.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: ‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK

paragraphs: As fuel prices across the United Kingdom reach their highest level since the onset of the conflict in Ukraine, inhabitants of remote Scottish islands are feeling the economic pressure more acutely than most. According to recent reports, mainland diesel has soared to a record peak of 200.01p per litre, while prices in the Hebrides and Shetland have climbed even higher, with certain forecourts charging upwards of 220p a litre.

This dramatic surge is driven primarily by a lack of local competition and the high cost of maritime shipping to isolated regions. For local residents, the ramifications are immediate and pervasive. Adam, a resident of North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, explained that the skyrocketing diesel prices have severely impacted his family. Because public transport options are extremely limited, he and his wife rely heavily on their vehicles for work and family duties, racking up roughly 15,000 miles a year. To offset these steep transportation costs, the family has been forced to buy cheaper food, as grocery prices are also heavily influenced by the haulage expenses passed down by delivery companies.

The financial strain extends far beyond daily commuting, affecting access to essential public services. Adam noted that when his daughter required a medical referral for a hearing test, the family had to travel more than 100 miles, book ferries, and stay in a hotel. Although partial reimbursements are available through patient travel schemes, the fixed allowances fall far short of the actual expenses, effectively stripping away the free nature of local healthcare access due to geographic isolation.

Meanwhile, residents in the Shetland archipelago express a deep sense of irony regarding their situation. Despite living right next to the major hubs of the North Sea oil and gas industry, locals face some of the highest energy and fuel poverty rates in the country. Bob, a local postman, pointed out that driving remains an absolute necessity for most workers since public bus schedules rarely align with standard employment hours. Many residents drive larger vehicles to cope with harsh local weather conditions, compounding the financial burden of the recent price hikes.

Younger workers are also feeling the pinch. Ryan, a 25-year-old resident of the Isle of Benbecula earning near minimum wage, described how soaring travel costs have forced him and his peers to cut back significantly on non-essential journeys. Leisure activities, such as visiting restaurants a half-hour drive away, have been put on hold. To combat the extreme prices, some islanders have resorted to filling jerry cans on the mainland during trips, bringing cheaper fuel back across the water—a tactic normally reserved for winter months when severe weather disrupts ferry deliveries and local pumps run dry. Despite the immense challenges of island life, residents emphasize that a strong sense of community and mutual support is helping them endure the ongoing economic squeeze.

facts.fact: Fuel prices in the UK have reached their highest level since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, with mainland diesel hitting a record high of 200.01p a litre.
In the Hebrides and Shetland, fuel prices have surged even higher due to a lack of competition and high shipping costs, with diesel exceeding 220p a litre.
Residents in remote Scottish islands report that soaring diesel costs are severely impacting their commutes, access to public services, and daily expenses like food.
